## Web Searcher: authoritative component-pattern and accessibility canon

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Your angle: **authoritative component-pattern and accessibility canon** — Area 2 plus the non-negotiable accessibility constraint. NN/g supplies documented failure modes (card-grid sameness, truncation, weak information scent), APG supplies exact keyboard/focus/inert semantics for drawers, sheets and modals, and Apple HIG / Material supply platform sheet conventions — all primary sources rather than listicles.
Search query: `Nielsen Norman Group and W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices guidance on modal dialog vs inline expansion vs routed page, drawer bottom sheet focus trap inert focus restore, progressive disclosure accordion details summary, card UI failure modes and alternatives to card grids`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).
- apify-ultimate-scraper: Universal AI-powered web scraper for any platform. Scrape data from Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, Google Maps, Google Search, Google Trends, Reddit, Airbnb, Yelp, and 15+ more platforms. Use for lead generation, brand monitoring, competitor analysis, influencer discovery, trend research, content analytics, audience analysis, review analysis, SEO intelligence, recruitment, or any data extraction task.

Also use when the user says "write copy for," "improve this copy," "rewrite this page," "marketing copy," "headline help," or "CTA copy." For email copy, see email-sequence. For popup copy, see popup-cro.

- image-to-code: Elite website image-to-code skill for Codex. For visually important web tasks, it must first generate the design image(s) itself, deeply analyze them, then implement the website to match them as closely as possible. In Codex, it must prefer large, readable, section-specific images instead of tiny compressed boards, generate fresh standalone images for sections or detail views instead of cropping old ones, avoid lazy under-generation, avoid cards-inside-cards-inside-cards UI, and keep the hero clean, spacious, readable, and visible on a small laptop.

By default, screens should be shown inside a subtle premium iPhone or similar phone mockup with a visible frame, while the main focus stays on the app content itself. This skill generates images only. It does not write code.

CRITICAL OUTPUT RULE — generate ONE separate horizontal image FOR EVERY section. A landing page with 8 sections produces 8 images. Never compress multiple sections into one image. I found comprehensive information about the W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices dialog modal pattern. Here's what the search results show:

## Key Dialog Modal Pattern Requirements

**Focus Management:**
When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element contained in the dialog, generally set on the first focusable element. When the modal closes, focus returns to the element that triggered it.

**Focus Trap:**
Modal dialogs contain their tab sequence, meaning Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog. Tab moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog, and if focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog.

**Escape Key:**
Escape closes the dialog.

**Inert Background Content:**
The aria-modal property introduced by ARIA 1.1 replaces aria-hidden for informing assistive technologies that content outside a dialog is inert. Content behind the modal must be hidden from assistive technology via aria-hidden="true" or the inert attribute.

**HTML Dialog Element Alternative:**
The HTML dialog element offers advantages with the browser handling focus being moved to the newly-opened modal dialog and keyboard focus returning to the invoking element when the modal dialog is closed.

The official source for these patterns is the [W3C WAI ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/).

Based on my search results, I've found relevant information about card UI design challenges. Here's what the research shows:

## Card UI Failure Modes

Truncation has become a well-known problem in card design, with text inside a box always presenting challenges on the web. Using text-overflow: ellipsis to truncate text results in only 3-4 visible words in a description, which is not very descriptive. When truncating at 150 characters and the sentence cuts off mid-thought, users lose interest in clicking, so excerpts should be written specifically for cards rather than auto-truncating content.

## Information Scent Issues

Cards are intended as high-information-scent outlines used to entice users to click through to further details contained on a separate page. However, this design goal can be undermined by poor implementation of content within the card.

## Other Card Grid Failure Modes

Cards with mismatched text lengths create awkward gaps and disrupt flow, which can be fixed with truncation, masonry layouts, or single-column views. Eye-tracking research by Nielsen Norman Group found that irregular card layouts cause people to scan in semirandom patterns, looking back and forth repeatedly, wasting time and mental energy. Not all data belongs in cards—tables are better for dense information and continuous layouts are better for linear flows like forms.

## Accessibility Failures

Wrapping the entire card in a single link tag is the single most common card accessibility failure, as it makes screen readers announce all card content as one continuous, unstructured string.

Based on the Nielsen Norman Group research, here are the key findings about progressive disclosure, accordions on desktop, and modal overlays:

## Progressive Disclosure

Progressive disclosure defers advanced or rarely used features to a secondary screen, making applications easier to learn and less error-prone.

## Accordions on Desktop

On desktop, use accordions for content-heavy pages where users will not need to access content under several accordions. Accordions are a type of progressive disclosure where the heading provides a concise overview of the topic and the panel is hidden by default, offering supplementary details to those who are interested.

The benefits of accordions include: Accordions display information one section at a time and hide information that is not relevant to the user, simplifying the page and lowering users' cognitive load.

## When to Avoid Overlays and Use Accordions Instead

When considering modal overlays, Nielsen Norman Group recommends an alternative approach: Designers should stay away from overlays whenever possible and instead attempt to use a different design component like an accordion or a full page. 

Additionally, accordions are an especially good idea when the overlay contains only relatively little content that does not require scrolling.

If overlays must be used, create clear signifiers that allow users to differentiate them from regular pages and display only limited content inside the overlay.

I found relevant information comparing Apple's Human Interface Guidelines with Material Design 3 regarding sheets and navigation components. Here are the key findings:

## Bottom Sheets

Bottom sheets in Material Design are used to present supplementary content without navigating to a new screen. In contrast, Apple's HIG recommends using a nonmodal view when you want to show additional options or tools without interrupting the main task.

A bottom sheet is a sheet of UI elements that slides up from the bottom of the screen and is most often used for displaying additional options or information that is related to the current task.

## Sheets in Apple HIG

A sheet helps people perform a scoped task that's closely related to their current context. More specifically, Apple's sheets component covers when to use a sheet versus a full-screen modal, detent configurations for the resizable sheet introduced in iOS 16, and how to handle navigation stacks inside sheets without breaking expected swipe-to-dismiss behavior.

## Navigation Components

Google provides a comprehensive set of pre-built components like cards, sheets, and navigation drawers that developers can use consistently across applications.

A sidebar enables app navigation and provides quick access to top-level collections of content in your app or game.

Both design systems emphasize different navigation patterns, with Material Design including navigation drawers and Apple HIG emphasizing tab bars and sidebars for navigation.

Based on the Nielsen Norman Group research, I found relevant information about list view versus card/grid view layouts for category pages:

## Key Findings:

**List View Advantages:**
List view allows for easy sorting and is space efficient, making it particularly useful when users need to compare and filter multiple items efficiently.

**Card/Grid View Advantages:**
Card view is visually engaging and creates effective groupings. Research also indicates that if you have a small number of visually distinct categories to present, a grid of tappable images may be the easiest and fastest design for people to use, though these images must contain helpful details and be presented at a large enough size to be recognizable.

**Context Matters for Category Pages:**
The Nielsen Norman research emphasizes that there is an increased amount of product information on product listing pages, and as long as the information is well-curated and uncluttered, this trend allows users to make informed decisions about products without visiting each detail page.

**When Lists Outperform Cards:**
Lists tend to be more effective when space efficiency is critical, sorting and comparison are key user tasks, and you have many items to display. Cards work better for visually distinct categories or when you can include meaningful images with products.

I've completed the web search. Here's a summary of the findings related to MDN documentation on the inert attribute, dialog element, showModal, focus management, top layer, and accessibility:

## Key Findings:

**Dialog Element & Modal Dialogs:**
The HTML `<dialog>` element is used to create both modal and non-modal dialog boxes. Modal dialog boxes block interaction with other UI elements, making the rest of the page inert, while non-modal dialog boxes allow interaction with the rest of the page.

**showModal() Method:**
The showModal() method of the HTMLDialogElement interface displays the dialog as a modal dialog, over the top of any other dialogs or elements that might be visible. A modal dialog displays in the top layer, along with a ::backdrop pseudo-element.

**Inert Attribute & showModal():**
Elements inside the same document as the dialog, except the dialog and its descendants, become inert (as if the inert attribute is specified). Additionally, modal `<dialog>`s generated with showModal() escape inertness, meaning that they don't inherit inertness from their ancestors, but can be made inert by having the inert attribute explicitly set on themselves.

**Focus Management:**
When using HTMLDialogElement.showModal() to open a `<dialog>`, focus is set on the first nested focusable element. Explicitly indicating the initial focus placement by using the autofocus attribute will help ensure initial focus is set on the element deemed the best initial focus placement for any particular dialog.

**Accessibility Considerations:**
Dialog elements invoked by the showModal() method implicitly have aria-modal="true". An inert element, along with its descendants, gets removed from the tab order and accessibility tree.

results.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern — ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (W3C/WAI)
results.snippet: The primary normative-adjacent source for Area 2's non-negotiable accessibility constraint on drawers, sheets and modals. Specifies exactly what the pipeline must ship: role="dialog" + aria-modal="true", accessible name via aria-labelledby/aria-label, focus moved into the dialog on open (generally the first focusable element, or a specific element via autofocus), tab sequence contained so Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog and never escape it, Escape closes, and focus RESTORED to the invoking element on close. Also states that aria-modal (ARIA 1.1) replaces per-element aria-hidden for marking background content inert — the modern implementation being the `inert` attribute. Gives the same contract for non-modal dialogs, which is the correct base for side panels/drawers that should not trap focus. Directly usable as the acceptance checklist for any drawer/sheet/modal CRAFT.md entry.

results.title: Cards: UI-Component Definition — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/g's definitional article on cards, and the authoritative statement of the card's intended job and its documented failure modes. Defines a card as a high-information-scent container meant to entice a click through to a separate detail page — which makes weak information scent the diagnostic failure, not a matter of taste. Names when cards are the WRONG container: dense comparable data belongs in a table, linear flows (forms, sequences) belong in continuous layout. Companion NN/g eye-tracking work on irregular card layouts found users scan in semi-random back-and-forth patterns, wasting time and mental energy — the primary evidence against masonry/ragged card grids. Also the source of the truncation critique (excerpts must be authored for the card, not machine-truncated mid-thought). This is the citation that lets the repo write the card's "Fails" clause from research rather than opinion.

results.title: Bottom Sheets: Definition and UX Guidelines — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NN/g's dedicated treatment of the bottom-sheet/drawer family: what distinguishes modal from non-modal (persistent) sheets, detent/partial-height behavior, drag handles as the affordance that signals resizability, and when a sheet beats a full-screen change of context. Pairs with NN/g's "Accidental Dismissal of Overlays" finding that swipe/tap-outside dismissal silently destroys work on mobile — the sheet's characteristic failure mode, and the reason a sheet needs a visible, keyboard-reachable close control rather than gesture-only dismissal. Supplies the platform-neutral half of the sheet vocabulary the repo currently lacks; combine with the APG dialog pattern for the focus contract.

results.title: Accordions on Desktop: When and How to Use — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: Covers progressive disclosure as an actual decision rule rather than a slogan, and is the source for the modal-vs-inline-expansion-vs-page arbitration the survey needs. Positions accordions as progressive disclosure where the heading carries the summary and the panel the supplementary detail; recommends them for content-heavy pages where users will NOT need several panels at once (the failure mode being users forced to open many, which is worse than a plain long page). Crucially, NN/g's overlay guidance says to avoid overlays where possible and use an accordion or a full page instead, and reserve overlays for small non-scrolling content — a direct, citable ranking of inline expansion above modals. Maps cleanly onto the native, zero-JS `<details>/<summary>` implementation, so it is cheap against the sub-100KB shell budget.

results.title: <dialog> element — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: The web-native, budget-friendly implementation path for everything the APG dialog pattern requires, and the answer to "CSS/HTML-native (cheap) vs heavy runtime". showModal() promotes the dialog to the top layer, renders a ::backdrop pseudo-element (styleable, so the scrim can be designed rather than a generic black 50%), makes all other document content implicitly inert — removed from tab order AND the accessibility tree — sets aria-modal="true" implicitly, moves focus to the first focusable element (or `autofocus`), traps tab, handles Escape natively, and restores focus to the invoker on close. That is a full focus-trap/restore/inert stack for roughly zero JS bytes, replacing the usual focus-trap library. Note the caveat it documents: modal dialogs escape ancestor inertness, and initial focus placement should be declared explicitly with autofocus rather than left to the default.

results.title: Sheets — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The platform-convention source for the sheet family the angle calls for: a sheet is for a scoped task closely related to the current context, versus a full-screen modal for a self-contained task that warrants taking over. Documents detents (partial-height resizable sheets, iOS 16+), how to keep swipe-to-dismiss coherent when a navigation stack lives inside a sheet, and — relevant to the modal-vs-inline decision — Apple's preference for a NONMODAL view when showing extra options or tools without interrupting the main task. Flag for the repo: these are native-platform conventions, so a web portfolio borrows the mental model (detents, scoped task, drag-to-dismiss) but must re-supply keyboard operability, focus restore and inert background itself, since none of it comes free off-platform.
